text.text: We would expect that a higher proportion of stop trials should affect the parameter representing global stopping, that is, the finishing times of the stopping accumulator in the extended diffusion model for conflict tasks.
However, this manipulation should not affect other parameters, such as the controlled component of the evidence accumulation process or non-decision time.
Using our example of the paradigm that combines two attentional-control tasks, we may execute Step 7 by investigating the discriminant validity between this paradigm and a processing-speed task.
For instance, if we combine a Stroop task with a Simon task, a suitable processing-speed task may be a simple color identification task.
In this task, symbols may be presented on each trial in the center of the screen, and participants will be asked to identify the color of the symbols.
This processing-speed task is suitable because the stimuli, the response format and the decision requirements are comparable to those used in the Stroop-Simon paradigm.
The only difference consists of the absence of distracting features.

Therefore, if the Stroop-Simon paradigm captures more than processing speed, the correlations between this paradigm and the processing-speed task should be lower than the correlations observed between different paradigms combining attentional-control tasks.
This pattern would provide evidence for discriminant validity.

Task designs and pilotingOnce we have tested the different variations in the parameters on simulated performance and have identified the attentional-control parameters, we should create experimental manipulations where these attentional-control parameters affect actual task performance.

For example, if the simulations of Step 2 identify filtering as the relevant process in attentional control, we should create experimental manipulations where filtering affects performance in the tasks.
Ideally, in this Step 3, we should be able to design different versions of this task, for example using different stimulus materials.
In Step 4, we should be able, in a virtuous cycle, to pilot the different versions of the task and to model the data using a formal model.
Ultimately, this should allow us to reach a version of the task that yields a large behavioral effect.

According to the model, this effect should depend strongly on the degree of attentional control, so that differences in the size of the effect reflect individual differences in the attentional-control parameter(s).
In an optimal scenario of this step, there should be a large behavioral effect of attentional control at the group level.
At the same time, there should be enough variability in this behavioral effect at the individual level to result in good reliability.
Step 4 may also help to determine whether any behavioral measures capture attentional control sufficiently well.
Typically, response times and/or accuracy are used to measure performance.
From previous research (e.g., Draheim et al., 2019; Rey-Mermet et al., 2025), we know that some criteria are crucial in the selection of a good behavioral measure.

As discussed in previous sections, the behavioral measure should have low measurement error and high true variability, and it should take into account individual differences in the speed-accuracy trade-off.
A behavioral measure may ease the use of the task in more applied research.
It is to note that based on the current research outlined in the methodological challenges, Step 4 represents the most challenging component of our approach.

Steps 5 and 6: Parameter recovery and experimental validation using selective influence studies The next step -that is, Step 5 of the proposed approach -consists of assessing parameter recovery by simulating performance for the tasks developed in Steps 3 and 4 from the model.

These steps are based on previous research which provides several verbal definitions and formal models of attentional control.

Building on this previous work, the steps include the formal implementation of a verbal definition, a task design that is derived from a model, and selective-influence studies for empirically validating model parameters.
This changes what counts as a validated measure.
It is no longer a reliable measure that correlates with other measures.
Rather, a validated measure is a measure derived from model parameters that change as a function of attentional control.
Consequently, the dimensionality of attentional control is tested on competing model architectures rather than only by inspecting correlations.
